task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: measurement of adherence to recommended mix

historical_evidence.finding: The engine’s recommended play type outperformed the team’s highest‑volume play type in 69.8% of decisions, but the result was deemed an artifact due to construction/selection flaws and small sample size.

Ranked playsheet counter‑ranking did not show a clear predictive signal for which alternative scored better in the second half (Spearman rho ≈ -0.064, p ≈ 0.10), though a significant Kruskal‑Wallis test (p = 2.7e‑5) suggested heterogeneity.
The possession control index (PCI) incremental R² over ORtg was inflated due to leakage tracking, rendering the result an artifact.
A proxy engine for matchup‑conditioned play‑type selection showed only modest agreement with the production engine (13/79 = 16.5 %) and was limited by small sample and leakage.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Engine‑based play‑type recommendation vs team modal PT
failed_approaches.why: Construction/selection flaw (artifact), small sample, leakage lookahead, sample‐size power issues.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranked playsheet validation for predictive power of counter‑ranking
failed_approaches.why: Unclear mechanism, leakage, low measurement reliability, small sample, drift non‑stationarity.
Artifact due to leakage, mechanical floor.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Proxy engine for matchup‑conditioned PT picker
failed_approaches.why: Unclear mechanism, leakage, small sample, sample‑size power.

evidence_establishes: Partial evidence that a playsheet counter ranking can differentiate scoring outcomes when a defense drops a play type, but the predictive signal is weak and inconclusive.
evidence_does_not_establish: A robust, statistically powered link between adherence to a suppression‑conditional recommended mix and game‑level winning outcomes.
own_inferences: The current dataset (54 series) is likely underpowered to detect modest effects of adherence on win probability. The historical studies show significant leakage and measurement reliability problems when using engine‑derived recommendations, suggesting that any future test must tightly control for leakage and confounding. The definition of “suppression‑conditional recommended mix” is not standardized across studies, so operationalizing it consistently will be challenging.
uncertainties: Exact operational definition of adherence and suppression‑conditional mix; reliability of play‑type recommendations; extent of leakage in the current per‑game data; potential unmeasured confounders such as team strength and opponent defensive strategies.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved evidence reveals multiple methodological flaws (artifact, leakage, small sample) in prior attempts to link engine‑derived play‑type recommendations with outcomes, leading to a conclusion that the present question is highly risky and likely untestable with the available data.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 54 series provide insufficient power for detecting moderate effect sizes.
Adherence to a suppression‑conditional mix may be rare, limiting exposure variability.
Historical studies show low reliability of engine‑derived recommendations.
Engine decisions may incorporate future information, creating lookahead bias.
Defensive strategies evolve over seasons, violating stationarity.

prior_work.summary: Prior work has examined the predictive value of playsheet counter rankings on scoring outcomes, but not on winning outcomes, and found inconclusive evidence with methodological limitations.

risks.text: Small number of series limits statistical power.
Adherence to the recommended mix may occur infrequently.
Engine‑derived play‑type recommendations exhibit low reliability.
Potential lookahead bias in engine decisions.
Defensive strategies may change across seasons.
Team strength and opponent quality may confound the relationship between adherence and win probability.

design.estimand: Difference in win probability between games with high adherence to the suppression‑conditional recommended mix versus low adherence.
design.sample: All playoff series with complete per‑game data (n = 54)
design.power: Not achievable given current sample size; a future study would need >200 series
design.controls: Team offensive/defensive rating, opponent rating, game location, season phase
design.falsification: Test the same model on games where suppression is not recommended (e.g., high‑volume play types) to check for spurious associations
design.decision_rule: Reject null if p < 0.05 after adjustment for leakage and confounding
